newsitem.title: USA: Dlr rise a concern, though has benefits -Bergsten.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rise a concern, though has benefits -Bergsten.

text.p: The United States should be concerned about the continued rise of the dollar, although it does help the stretched economy in the short-run by keeping import prices down, an influential economist said on Tuesday.

Fred Bergsten, Director of the Institute for International Economics think tank, told Reuters that the strong dollar was storing up problems on the trade front by making U.S. exports less competitive on world markets.
He criticized the Clinton administration for what he termed "benign neglect" of the currency, although he stopped short of advocating an American effort to bring it back down.

"I'm not saying necessarily turning it around precipitously and driving it back down," he said. "But I would think at a minimum you better start constantly talking about these issues in the G7 (Group of Seven)."

He ridiculed European arguments that the dollar was undervalued, contrasting America's rising trade deficit and its large foreign debts with France's big surplus and Germany's status as the world's number two creditor nation.

Earlier, in a speech to the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, Bergsten predicted that the euro would turn out to be a "hard" currency after its launch in 1999 and would eventually rival the dollar as the world's key reserve currency.
"The euro will be a very hard currency from the outset," he said.

That is partly because the new European central bank will be free of political interference and will be anxious to establish its credibility as an inflation-fighter through a tight monetary policy, he said.
In contrast, Bergsten expects European governments to run relatively relaxed budget policies after 1999 as they seek to promote economic growth and combat high unemployment.

The policy mix of tight monetary and loose fiscal policy will be reminiscent of that followed by the United States in the early 1980's under former President Ronald Reagan, he added. The result then was a stronger dollar.
